cards.why: S3 Vectors became generally available in December 2025 and is a supported, low-cost store for infrequently queried knowledge bases, with the caveat that hierarchical chunking can exceed its per-vector metadata limit.

cards.prompt: The standalone ___ API applies a guardrail to arbitrary text, including output from a model not hosted on Bedrock.
cards.why: ApplyGuardrail decouples policy from inference, so the same PII and grounding policies can wrap a self-hosted model or a tool result. It is billed per text unit like inline guardrails.

cards.prompt: AgentCore Runtime terminates an idle session after ___ minutes by default (configurable via idleRuntimeSessionTimeout).
cards.why: 900 seconds idle and 28,800 seconds (8 hours) maximum lifetime are the defaults for microVM runtimes; the idle timer resets on each invocation, the lifetime timer does not.

explain.prompt: You have built MCP servers and agent loops by hand. How would AgentCore change how you deploy and secure an agent for a law firm?
explain.modelAnswer: Today my loop, my tool servers and my auth are code I host and patch. AgentCore splits that into managed pieces without forcing a framework. The loop itself keeps running as my container, but on AgentCore Runtime each user session gets its own microVM, so one reviewer's documents are never in the same process as another's, and sessions can run for hours for long document batches. Inbound auth moves to AgentCore Identity: the React app sends a Cognito JWT, Runtime validates it, and I stop writing token middleware. Outbound credentials, say the firm's document management system over OAuth, live in the Identity token vault with a three-legged consent flow instead of in environment variables. My existing MCP servers plug into Gateway, which also wraps Lambda functions and OpenAPI specs as MCP tools and enforces who may call what; Policy adds declarative rules on tool use. Memory gives me cross-session recall with retention controls, and Observability emits OpenTelemetry traces of every tool call, which is the audit trail a firm's GC wants. The cost is coupling to AWS and consumption pricing; the gain is that the dangerous parts, isolation and credentials, are no longer mine to get wrong.
rubric: Runtime: per-session microVM isolation, long sessions, framework agnostic
Identity for inbound JWT and outbound OAuth credentials in a vault
Gateway reusing existing MCP servers and wrapping Lambda or OpenAPI
Observability or Policy as audit and control
States the trade-off (lock-in, pricing)

explain.prompt: Using Bedrock features, explain how you would stop a contract-review agent from leaking personal data or inventing clauses.
explain.modelAnswer: Two risks, two layers. For personal data I attach a guardrail with sensitive information filters: standard PII types such as names, emails and national IDs set to mask on output, plus custom regex for client identifiers like matter numbers in the wrong context. The same guardrail runs on input so a user cannot smuggle a prompt attack past the system prompt; the content filter's prompt-attack category covers that. For invented clauses I use retrieval augmented generation through a Knowledge Base over the contract set, so the model answers from retrieved chunks with citations, and I enable contextual grounding checks on the guardrail: the response is scored for grounding against the retrieved passages and for relevance to the question, and anything below the threshold is blocked with a message that says the answer could not be supported. Temperature zero and a system prompt that demands quotations help but are not controls. Everything runs through an EU inference profile, invocation logging goes to a locked S3 bucket with the knowledge that blocked content appears there in plain text, so that bucket is as sensitive as the documents. I would then test the guardrail with a red-team set before any partner sees it.
rubric: Sensitive information filters with mask versus block, on input and output
Prompt attack filtering
RAG via Knowledge Base with citations
Contextual grounding checks and threshold behaviour
Notes the invocation log plaintext caveat or testing before rollout

scenarios.situation: A pan-European law firm's engagement letter states all processing stays within the EU. The team switched the agent to a global. inference profile last month to cut cost and avoid throttling. A client audit is scheduled in three weeks.
scenarios.question: What do you do?

options.text: Move to the eu. profile now, verify destination Regions with GetInferenceProfile, add an SCP that denies Bedrock outside EU Regions, and disclose the past month's routing to the firm.
options.why: The global profile may have processed data in the US or APAC; fixing the routing, proving it with the SCP and CloudTrail's inferenceRegion field, and disclosing is the only position that survives an audit.

options.text: Switch to a single-Region model id in eu-central-1 with provisioned throughput to avoid throttling.
options.why: It satisfies residency and capacity, but provisioned throughput is expensive and not every model is available in-Region on demand; the eu. profile usually achieves the same with less cost.

options.text: Keep the global profile and add a contract clause that AWS Regions are all equivalent under GDPR adequacy.
options.why: The engagement letter says EU, not 'adequate'; unilaterally reinterpreting a client's data residency commitment to save 10% is how a consulting firm loses the account.

nodes.title: The Target Architecture
nodes.tease: Your Terraform state holds the database password in plain text. Who can read that bucket today?

lesson.body:
A browser loads the React build from **CloudFront** with an OAC-protected **S3** bucket; the `/api/*` behavior forwards to an **API Gateway HTTP API** whose JWT authorizer validates Cognito tokens. A **VPC link** reaches an internal **ALB** fronting an **ECS Fargate** service in private subnets running the container from **ECR**. The task has two identities: the **task execution role** pulls the image and reads Secrets Manager; the **task role** is what your code assumes to call S3, Bedrock and OpenSearch. **RDS PostgreSQL** Multi-AZ sits in isolated subnets with its password in Secrets Manager. **OpenSearch** runs as a VPC domain or a Serverless collection behind a VPC endpoint. Documents live in an SSE-KMS bucket. **Bedrock** is reached through a `bedrock-runtime` interface endpoint with an `eu.` inference profile; the agent loop can run on **AgentCore Runtime** with Gateway exposing tools over MCP. ECR, Secrets Manager, CloudWatch Logs and S3 gateway endpoints let private subnets work without NAT.

**Terraform** provisions all of it. Current Terraform is 1.16.x under the BSL licence, with OpenTofu as the open fork. Remote state goes in S3 with `encrypt = true`, a KMS key, versioning and **`use_lockfile = true`** for native locking (since 1.10; the DynamoDB lock table is deprecated). State stores attributes in plain text, including any password you set yourself: restrict the bucket to pipeline roles, use `manage_master_user_password`, and prefer write-only arguments for secrets. Use modules per layer, one root per environment, and run plan and apply only from CodeBuild.

**Delivery** is a V2 **CodePipeline**: GitHub source via CodeConnections; CodeBuild tests, builds the ARM64 image, pushes to ECR and resolves the digest; Terraform plan; manual approval; apply and ECS deploy by digest; invalidate `/index.html`. Alarm on ALB 5xx, p99 latency, RDS `ReplicaLag` and Bedrock throttles; trace via ADOT to X-Ray. Cost levers: Fargate Spot in non-prod, zero-OCU Serverless minimums, batch inference.

cards.prompt: Your container code calls bedrock:InvokeModel and gets AccessDenied. Which role needs the permission?
options: The ECS task execution role
The ECS task role
The ALB's service-linked role
The CodeBuild service role
cards.why: Application code assumes the task role; the execution role is only used by the ECS agent to pull from ECR, read secrets and write logs. Granting Bedrock to the execution role is a common mistake that also widens the pull path's privileges.

cards.prompt: How should Terraform state be locked for the S3 backend today?
options: use_lockfile = true for S3-native locking
A DynamoDB table with a LockID partition key
No locking; CodeBuild serializes runs
A Consul backend
cards.why: Native S3 locking via a .tflock object arrived in Terraform 1.10 and DynamoDB locking is deprecated for removal. Relying on the pipeline to serialize ignores engineers running plan locally against the same state.

cards.prompt: You set the RDS master password as a Terraform variable from a .tfvars file. Where does the secret end up?
options: Only in the tfvars file
In the state file in plain text, readable by anyone with access to the state bucket
Nowhere; Terraform hashes sensitive values
In CloudTrail
cards.why: Marking a value sensitive only redacts CLI output; state stores it verbatim. Use manage_master_user_password so RDS generates it into Secrets Manager, or ephemeral resources and write-only arguments, and lock the state bucket down.

cards.prompt: Which request path keeps the ECS tasks without public IPs and off the internet?
options: CloudFront to a public ALB in public subnets
CloudFront to API Gateway HTTP API, VPC link to an internal ALB, Fargate tasks in private subnets with VPC endpoints for ECR, S3, Secrets Manager and Bedrock
CloudFront directly to Fargate task IPs
API Gateway Lambda proxy to tasks over the internet
cards.why: The VPC link is the private bridge from the gateway into the VPC; interface and gateway endpoints replace the NAT gateway for AWS APIs. A public ALB works but exposes a second entry point that bypasses the gateway's authorizer.

cards.prompt: Fargate tasks in private subnets can pull images from ECR without a NAT gateway if you add ECR api and dkr interface endpoints plus an S3 gateway endpoint.
cards.why: ECR stores layers in S3, so the S3 gateway endpoint is the piece people forget; without it pulls hang. Add CloudWatch Logs and Secrets Manager endpoints too, or the task fails before your code runs.

cards.prompt: DynamoDB-based state locking is still the recommended default for Terraform's S3 backend.
cards.why: It is deprecated; use_lockfile is the recommended path and both can be set during migration. Many tutorials and modules still create the table, which is how outdated patterns end up in new repos.

cards.prompt: Terraform 1.10 introduced S3-native state locking through the ___ backend argument.
cards.why: It writes a .tflock object next to the state, so the role needs GetObject, PutObject and DeleteObject on that key. Missing DeleteObject leaves stale locks that look like a crashed colleague.

cards.prompt: To call Bedrock from private subnets without internet access, create a VPC ___ endpoint (PrivateLink) for bedrock-runtime.
cards.why: Interface endpoints are ENIs with private IPs for AWS APIs; only S3 and DynamoDB use gateway endpoints. An endpoint policy can also pin which models and inference profiles the VPC may invoke.

explain.prompt: Draw the request path for 'summarize this deposition' end to end, and name every IAM identity involved.
explain.modelAnswer: The reviewer clicks summarize in React. The browser holds a Cognito access token, obtained through the hosted UI; CloudFront serves the app from S3 using its origin access control, which is the first identity, the CloudFront service principal allowed by the bucket policy. The POST to /api/matters/42/summaries goes through CloudFront's /api behavior to the HTTP API, whose JWT authorizer validates the token with no identity of its own. API Gateway invokes the VPC link to the internal ALB and the Fargate task. Here two roles matter: the task execution role pulled the image from ECR and injected the database secret, and the task role is what the code now uses. With the task role the service checks matter membership in Postgres over a connection authenticated with the Secrets Manager password, fetches the deposition from the documents bucket, which also needs kms:Decrypt on the client key, retrieves chunks from OpenSearch where a fine-grained access control role mapped to the task role filters by matter, and calls bedrock:InvokeModel through the interface endpoint using the eu. inference profile with a guardrail. The summary is written back to Postgres and the audit event to the locked audit bucket. Everything is logged to CloudTrail under the task role, which is the trail the firm's GC can follow.
rubric: CloudFront OAC principal and S3 bucket policy
Cognito token validated by the JWT authorizer, VPC link to internal ALB
Distinguishes task execution role from task role
Task role permissions for S3 plus KMS, OpenSearch via FGAC mapping, Bedrock via endpoint
Secrets Manager for the database credential
Audit trail via CloudTrail or audit bucket

explain.prompt: What does 'production-ready' mean for this stack? Give me your checklist.
explain.modelAnswer: Six headings. Identity and secrets: Cognito in front, least-privilege task role, RDS password managed by Secrets Manager, no secret in Terraform state, SCP restricting Regions. Network: private subnets, VPC endpoints instead of NAT where possible, WAF on CloudFront, security groups that only allow ALB to tasks and tasks to the database. Data: SSE-KMS with customer keys, versioning, Object Lock on audit logs, Multi-AZ Postgres with 35-day backups and a tested point-in-time restore, OpenSearch fine-grained access control with document-level security. Delivery: everything in Terraform with remote locked state, a V2 pipeline with plan, approval and apply, images pinned by digest and scanned with Inspector, rollback via task definition revisions. Operations: structured logs, traces, alarms on 5xx, latency, replica lag and Bedrock throttling, a runbook for failover, and a cost budget with alerts. Finally the AI-specific items: EU inference profile, guardrails for PII and grounding, evaluation set for answer quality, and limits on agent tool use. If I had to pick the three that distinguish a demo from production, they are tested restores, enforced isolation at the data layer, and a pipeline nobody can bypass.
rubric: Identity and secrets management, least privilege
Network isolation (private subnets, endpoints, WAF, security groups)
Data protection and recovery (KMS, Multi-AZ, backups tested, Object Lock, FGAC)
Infrastructure as code and pipeline with approval, digest pinning and scanning
Observability, alarms and runbooks, cost controls
AI-specific controls (residency, guardrails, evaluation)

scenarios.situation: The team keeps Terraform state in a shared S3 bucket readable by the whole engineering group and runs terraform apply from laptops with admin credentials. A junior engineer, following a 2022 blog post, proposes adding a DynamoDB lock table to 'make it safe'.
scenarios.question: What do you do?

options.text: Switch to use_lockfile, restrict the state bucket to the pipeline's plan and apply roles with KMS and versioning, move RDS to manage_master_user_password so state holds no password, and make CodeBuild the only place apply runs.
options.why: Locking was never the real risk; the plaintext password in a widely readable bucket and unaudited laptop applies were. Native locking is the current recommendation and the pipeline gives the audit trail the client will ask for.

options.text: Add the DynamoDB lock table as proposed, but also restrict the bucket policy and enable versioning.
options.why: Tightening the bucket is the important part; the DynamoDB table works but is deprecated, and laptop applies with admin credentials remain an unaudited path.

options.text: Add the lock table and move on; the bucket is internal so readability is fine.
options.why: Internal is not a security boundary for a database password; any engineer, or any compromised laptop, can read production credentials out of state.

questions.prompt: A prototype works in a demo: React app, a Python service calling Bedrock, documents in a bucket. The partner wants it in front of a law firm in six weeks. What do you do to make it production-ready?
questions.modelOutline: Open with the three things that separate demo from production: enforced isolation at the data layer, recoverability, and a pipeline nobody bypasses. Then walk the stack. Identity: Cognito plus JWT authorizer, matter-level authorization in the service, least-privilege task role, secrets in Secrets Manager, nothing in state. Network: private subnets, VPC link to internal ALB, endpoints, WAF. Data: SSE-KMS with customer keys, versioning, Object Lock for audit, Multi-AZ Postgres with tested PITR, OpenSearch FGAC with document-level security. Delivery: Terraform with locked remote state, V2 pipeline with plan, approval and apply, digest-pinned scanned images, rollback. Operations: logs, traces, alarms, runbooks, cost budget. AI: EU inference profile, guardrails for PII and grounding, an evaluation set, tool-use limits. Close with sequencing for six weeks and what you would cut.

Authentication and matter-level authorization with least-privilege roles

Isolation enforced in the engine (FGAC/DLS or equivalent), not only in the UI
Infrastructure as code and a gated pipeline with digest pinning and scanning
Observability, alarms and runbooks

questions.prompt: Whiteboard the deployment for this app using the services we named: React, API Gateway, ECS, ECR, RDS Postgres, OpenSearch, S3, Bedrock, Terraform and CodePipeline. Talk me through the diagram.

Bedrock via private endpoint with EU inference profile and guardrails

questions.prompt: The client's CISO asks: where does privileged data flow, where is it stored at rest, and who can read it at each point? Answer for every service in the stack.
questions.modelOutline: Go hop by hop. Browser to CloudFront: TLS, WAF, no document content cached because /api is CachingDisabled. API Gateway: validates JWT, logs metadata not bodies. ECS task: in memory only, task role is the only reader of downstream stores. S3 documents: SSE-KMS customer key, key policy and bucket policy list the task role and a break-glass role, CloudTrail data events record every GetObject. RDS: encrypted volume, password in Secrets Manager rotated weekly, access from the task security group only. OpenSearch: encrypted at rest and in transit, FGAC roles with document-level security per matter. Bedrock: no training on prompts, eu. inference profile, invocation logs in a locked bucket and the plaintext caveat. Audit bucket: Object Lock compliance mode. Terraform state: KMS, restricted to pipeline roles, no secrets. People: SSO roles, no long-lived keys, SCP restricting Regions. Close with how you would prove it: Access Analyzer, CloudTrail queries, a quarterly restore test.
